passages.happening: “My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you will not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate before the Father—Jesus Christ, the Righteous One. He Himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world” (verses 1-2).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 1 ended with honesty about sin and the promise of forgiveness. Someone might draw the wrong lesson: if God forgives, sin does not matter. John blocks that at once. ‘I am writing these things to you so that you will not sin.’ The aim is a holy life.

But he does not leave his readers there. ‘If anyone does sin, we have an advocate.’ The Greek word is paraklētos, someone called alongside to help, often a friend who spoke for a person in a legal setting. John's Gospel uses the same word for the Holy Spirit, ‘another Advocate’ (John 14:16). Here the advocate is Jesus himself, speaking to the Father for those who have sinned.

He is not a lawyer arguing that his client is innocent. He is ‘the Righteous One’, and he is himself ‘the atoning sacrifice for our sins’. The word is hilasmos. In ordinary Greek, words of this family were used for turning away anger or making amends. In the twentieth century C. H. Dodd argued that in the Bible it means the removal of sin, and Leon Morris argued that it also means satisfying God's just anger. Many now see both: God himself provides the sacrifice that takes away sin, and so turns away his judgment.

And the reach of that sacrifice is wide: ‘not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world’. John's readers had just seen a group leave, claiming a better knowledge. John will not let anyone think that the cross belongs to a small circle.
passages.ot:
The picture of a sacrifice for sin comes from Israel's worship. On the Day of Atonement the high priest offered a sacrifice and entered God's presence for the people: “So he shall make atonement for the Most Holy Place because of the impurities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins” (Leviticus 16:16).

Isaiah's servant would bear the sins of many and speak for them: “Yet He bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12).

And Job, in his suffering, longed for someone in heaven to speak for him: “Even now my witness is in heaven, and my advocate is on high” (Job 16:19).
passages.hard:
‘Not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world.’ Does this mean everyone will be saved? And for whom did Christ die?

Christians agree that this verse does not teach that everyone will be saved, since the same letter says, “whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life” (5:12). Beyond that, they read it in different ways.

Many, including Arminian and much of Lutheran and evangelical thought, read it as teaching that Christ died for every person without exception. On this reading his sacrifice is enough for all and offered to all, and it is received by faith.

Those who hold to particular or definite atonement, common in Reformed theology, read ‘the whole world’ as people from every nation, not only John's own churches or the people of Israel. They point to John 11:52, which speaks of Jesus dying to gather into one ‘the scattered children of God’.

Some take a middle view: Christ's death is enough for all, and it is effective for those who believe.

These notes do not choose. All agree on John's point. The cross is not the private possession of one group. Its reach is as wide as the world, and no one who comes to Christ will find that his sacrifice was not meant for them.
passages.asks: Ask whether you have ever treated God's forgiveness as a reason to take sin lightly. Ask what it means to you that Jesus speaks to the Father on your behalf when you fail. And ask whom you are tempted to think the cross is not for.

passages.t: Knowing God, keeping his word, loving your brother
passages.happening:
“By this we can be sure that we have come to know Him: if we keep His commandments. If anyone says, ‘I know Him,’ but does not keep His commandments, he is a liar, and the truth is not in him. But if anyone keeps His word, the love of God has been truly perfected in him. By this we know that we are in Him: Whoever claims to abide in Him must walk as Jesus walked” (verses 3-6).

“Beloved, I am not writing to you a new commandment, but an old one, which you have had from the beginning. This commandment is the message you have heard. Then again, I am also writing to you a new commandment, which is true in Him and also in you. For the darkness is fading and the true light is already shining” (verses 7-8).

“If anyone claims to be in the light but hates his brother, he is still in the darkness. Whoever loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no cause of stumbling in him. But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness. He does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (verses 9-11).
passages.hearers:
Three more claims, three more tests. ‘I know Him.’ ‘I abide in Him.’ ‘I am in the light.’ Each is checked against life.

The first test is obedience. Knowing God is not only knowing facts about him. It shows in keeping his commands. A person who says ‘I know Him’ and ignores what he says has not understood who God is. The second test sets the bar high and plain: ‘walk as Jesus walked’. The Christian life is the copy of a person.

Then John speaks of a commandment that is both old and new. It is old because his readers had it ‘from the beginning’, from the first time they heard the gospel. It is new because in Jesus it came with a new measure and a new power. Jesus said, “A new commandment I give you: Love one another” (John 13:34). And it is new because a new age has begun: ‘the darkness is fading and the true light is already shining’.

The third test is love. A person who says he is in the light and hates his brother is still in the dark. ‘Brother’ here means a fellow believer, a sister as much as a brother. Hatred does not only hurt the other person. It blinds the one who hates. He ‘does not know where he is going’. Love, by contrast, leaves nothing in the way to trip over.

These tests were not written to make anxious people more anxious. They were written so that John's readers could see clearly. People who claimed to know God and despised their brothers had left. Those who stayed and loved were walking in the light.
passages.ot:
The ‘old commandment’ goes back to the law: “Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against any of your people, but love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD” (Leviticus 19:18). The same chapter forbids hatred: “You must not harbor hatred against your brother in your heart” (Leviticus 19:17).

Knowing God and keeping his word belong together in the prophets: “He took up the cause of the poor and needy, and so it went well with him. Is this not what it means to know Me?” declares the LORD (Jeremiah 22:16).

And the light that is already shining recalls Isaiah: “The people walking in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah 9:2).
passages.asks: Ask what it would look like to ‘walk as Jesus walked’ in one ordinary part of your day. Ask whether there is someone in your church you hold a grudge against or quietly despise. And ask whether that is blinding you to where you are going.

passages.t: To children, fathers and young men
passages.happening:
“I am writing to you, little children, because your sins have been forgiven through His name. I am writing to you, fathers, because you know Him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one” (verses 12-13).

“I have written to you, children, because you know the Father. I have written to you, fathers, because you know Him who is from the beginning. I have written to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one” (verses 13-14).
passages.hearers:
After hard tests, John stops to encourage. These verses have a rhythm, almost like a poem: six lines, three of them saying ‘I am writing’, three saying ‘I have written’.

Who are the children, fathers and young men? Readers have taken them in three ways. Some think of three age groups in the church. Some think ‘little children’ is John's name for everyone, as it is elsewhere in the letter, with ‘fathers’ and ‘young men’ as two groups among them. Others think of three stages of growth in faith. On any reading, John speaks to the whole church.

And notice what he says. He does not write because they are failing. He writes because their sins have been forgiven, because they know God, because they have already overcome the evil one. This is not flattery. It is reassurance for people who had been made to feel second-class by those who left. John tells them what is already true of them.

Each group hears something fitting. The children, that they are forgiven and know the Father. The fathers, mature in faith, that they know the One who is from the beginning. The young men, that they are strong because God's word lives in them, and that they have won the battle against evil.
passages.ot:
John's ‘fathers’ who know ‘Him who is from the beginning’ recall Israel's call to hand the faith down: “Tell it to your children; let your children tell it to their children, and their children to the next generation” (Joel 1:3).

The strength that comes from God's word living within is the psalm's: “I have hidden Your word in my heart that I might not sin against You” (Psalm 119:11). And “How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to Your word” (Psalm 119:9).
passages.asks: Ask which line of these verses you most need to hear today. Ask whether you know that your sins are forgiven ‘through His name’. And ask whom in your church you could encourage by telling them what God has already done in them.

passages.happening: “Do not love the world or anything in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life—is not from the Father but from the world. The world is passing away, along with its desires; but whoever does the will of God remains forever” (verses 15-17).
passages.hearers:
‘The world’ is a word John uses in more than one way. Sometimes it means all people, as when he says Jesus is the sacrifice for ‘the whole world’ (verse 2) or ‘the Savior of the world’ (4:14). Here it means something else: the whole way of life that is organised without God and against him. Loving that world competes with loving the Father.

John names three things in it. ‘The desires of the flesh’: appetites that want to rule. ‘The desires of the eyes’: wanting what we see. ‘The pride of life’: the boast that comes from what we have or who we are. Many readers have noticed how closely these match Eve's temptation in Eden, where the fruit was good for food, pleasing to the eyes and desirable for wisdom.

And John gives a reason that is simple and sobering. ‘The world is passing away, along with its desires.’ What seems so solid will not last. But ‘whoever does the will of God remains forever’.
passages.ot:
Many readers hear Eden behind these verses: “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes, and that it was desirable for obtaining wisdom, she took the fruit and ate it” (Genesis 3:6).

The prophets and psalms set what passes against what lasts: “The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever” (Isaiah 40:8). And “Turn my eyes away from worthless things; revive me with Your word” (Psalm 119:37).
passages.hard:
Does ‘do not love the world’ mean Christians should despise the earth, their bodies, or the people around them?

No. The same John wrote, “For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son” (John 3:16). There ‘the world’ means people whom God loves. Here it means a way of life set against God. Christians are not told to stop loving people, to scorn God's good creation, or to withdraw from ordinary life.

In fact the teachers John was opposing seem to have looked down on the body and the physical world. John's answer to them was a Christ who came in the flesh. Loving God and refusing the world's pride does not mean hating what God made. It means not letting appetite, envy or pride take the place that belongs to God.
passages.asks: Ask which of the three, the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes or the pride of life, pulls hardest on you. Ask what you are building your life on that is ‘passing away’. And ask what it would mean today to do the will of God.

passages.happening:
“Children, it is the last hour; and just as you have heard that the antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have appeared. This is how we know it is the last hour” (verse 18).

“They went out from us, but they did not belong to us. For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us. But their departure made it clear that none of them belonged to us” (verse 19).

“You, however, have an anointing from the Holy One, and all of you know the truth. I have not written to you because you lack knowledge of the truth, but because you have it, and because no lie comes from the truth. Who is the liar, if it is not the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son. Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father, but whoever confesses the Son has the Father as well” (verses 20-23).
passages.hearers:
Here, for the first time, John names the crisis behind the letter. A group had left the churches. ‘They went out from us.’ Those who left seem to have claimed a higher, more spiritual knowledge. Those who stayed were left hurt and unsure.

John explains what has happened. His readers had been taught that ‘the antichrist is coming’, perhaps from Jesus' warnings about false Christs and false prophets (Mark 13:22) and Paul's teaching about ‘the man of lawlessness’ (2 Thessalonians 2:3). John says that many antichrists have already appeared, and he means the teachers who had left. Their teaching denied that Jesus is the Christ. In this letter that is probably not a Jewish denial that Jesus was the Messiah. It is more likely a denial that the man Jesus was himself the divine Christ, the kind of teaching Irenaeus later reported of Cerinthus.

Then John turns to those who stayed. They are not lacking. ‘You have an anointing from the Holy One, and all of you know the truth.’ Kings, priests and prophets were anointed with oil in Israel. Most readers take this anointing as the Holy Spirit, given to every believer; some take it as the gospel word they received. Either way, the people who stayed do not need the secret knowledge the others claimed.

And John's last line is the heart of it. To deny the Son is to lose the Father. To confess the Son is to have the Father too. What a person believes about Jesus is not a side issue. It is the question of whether he has God at all.
passages.ot:
Israel's law warned against prophets who drew people from the true God: “you must not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer. For the LORD your God is testing you” (Deuteronomy 13:3).

Anointing set people apart for God's work. Samuel anointed David, “and the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward” (1 Samuel 16:13). And the prophet said of the coming servant, “The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me” (Isaiah 61:1).

The psalm speaks of the Father and his anointed Son together: “The kings of the earth take their stand and the rulers gather together, against the LORD and against His Anointed One” (Psalm 2:2).
passages.hard:
Who is ‘the antichrist’? And what does it mean that those who left ‘did not belong to us’?

Begin with what John himself says. The word ‘antichrist’ appears in the Bible only in the letters of John. His readers had heard that ‘the antichrist is coming’. John tells them that ‘many antichrists have appeared’, that the antichrist is ‘the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ’ and ‘denies the Father and the Son’, and, in chapter 4, that ‘the spirit of the antichrist’ is ‘already in the world’. In his letters, then, antichrists are teachers who deny the truth about Jesus, and the spirit behind that teaching. These had been inside the church.

Many Christians also expect a final figure of evil before Christ returns, and link John's word with Paul's ‘man of lawlessness’ and the beast of Revelation. Others read these passages as speaking of a power of rebellion that takes shape again and again. The notes on 2 Thessalonians 2 set out the readings.

Over the centuries people have often named someone of their own day as the antichrist, or tied the figure to an emperor, a pope, a sultan or a dictator. Such identifications have been made many times, and they have often frightened believers and turned Christians against one another. These notes make none. They identify the antichrist with no living person, office, church, nation, leader or movement. John's own use points another way: test every teacher by what he confesses about Jesus Christ, and look first to your own heart.

As for those who ‘went out from us’, Christians read verse 19 in line with their wider views. Many Reformed and Calvinist churches see in it the perseverance of the saints: those who finally fall away show that they never truly belonged. Arminian and Wesleyan Christians hold that a true believer can turn away in unbelief and be lost, and read the verse as describing these particular teachers. Lutheran and Catholic teaching hold that grace can be lost, and each points the troubled back to Christ. These notes do not choose.

This verse is about teachers who denied Christ, not about every person who has left a church. People leave churches for many reasons, some of them because they were hurt. That is not what John is speaking of.
passages.asks: Ask what you believe about Jesus, and whether it is the Jesus who came in the flesh. Ask whether you have been made to feel that your faith is second-class, and hear John: ‘all of you know the truth’. And ask how you can test what you hear without becoming suspicious of everyone.

passages.happening:
“As for you, let what you have heard from the beginning remain in you. If it does, you will also remain in the Son and in the Father. And this is the promise that He Himself made to us: eternal life” (verses 24-25).

“I have written these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you. And as for you, the anointing you received from Him remains in you, and you do not need anyone to teach you. But just as His true and genuine anointing teaches you about all things, so remain in Him as you have been taught” (verses 26-27).
passages.hearers:
‘Remain’ is the word that runs through this passage. In Greek it is menō, to stay, to abide, to remain. It appears again and again in this chapter. Those who left did not remain. Those who stayed are to keep remaining: in what they heard from the beginning, in the Son, in the Father.

‘From the beginning’ matters. The teachers who left offered something new and more advanced. John says the way forward is not to run after the new thing but to hold fast to what was first given. And holding to it is not dull. It carries a promise: ‘eternal life’.

Then a line that has puzzled many. ‘You do not need anyone to teach you.’ Does John mean Christians need no teachers? He is writing to teach them as he says it. His point is aimed at the deceivers, who claimed that ordinary believers needed their special teaching to know God. John says no. The Spirit God has given already teaches them the truth. They do not need a secret knowledge from those who left.
passages.ot:
John's promise echoes the new covenant: “No longer will each man teach his neighbor or his brother, saying, ‘Know the LORD,’ because they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest, declares the LORD” (Jeremiah 31:34).

The prophets promised God's Spirit to all his people: “And afterward, I will pour out My Spirit on all people” (Joel 2:28).

And Isaiah: “Then all your sons will be taught by the LORD, and great will be their prosperity” (Isaiah 54:13).
passages.hard:
‘You do not need anyone to teach you.’ Does this mean Christians do not need pastors, teachers or the church?

No. The New Testament gives the church teachers as Christ's gift (Ephesians 4:11), and John himself is teaching in this very letter. His words are aimed at the deceivers, who said that believers lacked something only they could give. John answers that every believer has the Spirit, and that what they received from the beginning is enough. They need no one to add a secret teaching to the gospel.

Christians have also drawn from this verse that the Spirit helps every believer, not only experts, to recognise the truth. That is not a licence to ignore wise teachers or the church's long reading of Scripture. It is a guard against anyone who claims that faith in Christ is not enough without them.
passages.asks: Ask what you have heard ‘from the beginning’ that you need to hold onto now. Ask whether anyone has made you feel that you need their special knowledge to know God. And ask how you can stay teachable while trusting that the Spirit has been given to you too.

passages.happening: “And now, little children, remain in Christ, so that when He appears, we may be confident and unashamed before Him at His coming. If you know that He is righteous, you also know that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of Him” (verses 28-29).
passages.hearers:
John ends the chapter by looking ahead. Christ will appear. When he does, John wants his little children to be ‘confident and unashamed’.

The word for ‘coming’ is parousia, which in the Greek world could mean the arrival of a ruler on a visit. The question is not whether he will come but how we will stand when he does. John's answer is the same word again: remain. Those who stay in Christ need not hide.

Then a new thought that leads into chapter 3. ‘Born of Him.’ Those who do what is right show the family likeness of the righteous God. This is not how they become his children. It is how their being his children shows.
passages.ot:
Being unashamed before God is the psalm's hope: “Those who look to Him are radiant with joy; their faces shall never be ashamed” (Psalm 34:5).

And the righteousness of God is Israel's confession: “For the LORD is righteous; He loves justice. The upright will see His face” (Psalm 11:7).
passages.asks: Ask how you would feel if Christ appeared today, and why. Ask what it means for you to ‘remain in Christ’ this week. And ask where the family likeness of God shows in your life, and where it does not yet.
